title: Tzav: ear, thumb, toe (Leviticus 8:23–24)
hook: priests are anointed on the ear, the thumb and the big toe: hear, do, walk
tomorrow: Tzav: seven days at the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, todah, the thanks offering brought after a rescue. Your line was thanks outlasts everything. Today, the priests are ordained, with three surprising marks.

Designing a ceremony to make someone a priest, where would you put the mark? The forehead, maybe, like a crown. The heart. The hands that will do the work. The Torah picks three places few would guess: the edge of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot. It sounds almost comic, until you stop and ask what those three have in common, and what they leave out.
screen: `WHERE WOULD YOU PUT THE MARK?` → `NOT THE HEAD, NOT THE HEART.` → `EAR, THUMB, BIG TOE.`

segments.voice: It's the week of the priests' ordination. Moses, acting as priest himself for these days, brings a ram called the ram of consecration and takes some of its blood. He puts it "upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot," then does the same for each of Aaron's sons. The Torah doesn't explain the choice. Commentators have read it as a map of a life of service. The ear, to listen: to God, and to the people who come with their troubles. The hand, to do the work. The foot, to walk the right path and go where you're needed. Listening first, then doing, then walking, and the order runs from top to bottom: the whole body, claimed for service. Then a surprise from later in Leviticus. The same marking, ear, thumb and toe, is done for someone else: a person healed from the skin affliction called tzara'at, who had been living outside the camp and is now coming home. The priest starting his service and the outcast returning to the community receive the same three touches. Some readers take the pairing as a sign the marking isn't about rank, but about a person beginning again, with ears, hands and feet given a new purpose.
screen: `THE RAM OF CONSECRATION.` · `EAR, THUMB AND BIG TOE.` · `LISTEN, THEN DO, THEN WALK.` · `THE SAME MARK FOR ONE RETURNING.` · then, large: `LISTEN, DO, WALK.`

segments.voice: Touch your right ear gently and ask what you need to listen for today, and who needs you to listen. Touch your right thumb and ask what your hands should do; then press your right big toe to the floor and ask where you need to go, or not go. Take a breath with each, then sit with all three, ready.
Tzav. Command. The portion where the priests are ordained, marked on the right ear, the right thumb and the right big toe.
Your line: listen, do, walk. Ear, hand and foot, all given to the work. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why mark a new priest on the ear, thumb and big toe? It seems so random.
options: Many read it as a map of service: an ear to listen, a hand to work, a foot to walk.
They marked the places that would touch the altar fire, to protect them from burns.
It was a sign of rank, so only priests ever received those three marks.
chat.meaning: The Torah doesn't explain it, but commentators read ear, thumb and toe as listening, doing and walking. A healed person coming home gets the same marks.
